hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: When would you choose an L7 load balancer over an L4 one?
options: When routing depends on HTTP details such as path, host, headers or cookies
When you only need raw TCP throughput
When you want no TLS termination
When backends are stateless databases only
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: L4 balances on IP and port and is fast and simple. L7 understands the request, so it can route /api and /static differently, do canary releases and terminate TLS, at higher CPU cost.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: Why is least-connections often better than round robin for long-lived requests?
options: Round robin ignores how busy each backend currently is
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: If requests vary in duration, equal request counts don't mean equal load. Least-connections (or least-latency) balances actual in-flight work.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: Cache-aside (lazy loading): what happens on a cache miss?
options: The application reads the database, then writes the value into the cache
The cache reads the database itself
The database pushes the data to the cache
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: The app owns the logic. It's simple and resilient to cache failure, but the first read is slow and the data can be stale until TTL or invalidation.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: Write-through vs write-back caching: which risks losing data if the cache crashes?
options: Write-back, since writes are acknowledged before reaching the database
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Write-back batches writes to the database asynchronously for speed. Write-through writes to cache and database synchronously, trading latency for safety.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: Which is the hardest problem in caching according to the well-known quote?
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Keeping cached copies consistent with the source of truth is hard: use TTLs, event-driven invalidation or versioned keys.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: What is a cache stampede (thundering herd)?
options: Many requests miss simultaneously for an expired hot key and all hit the database
The cache runs out of memory
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: Mitigate with request coalescing (single-flight), a short lock on regeneration, jittered TTLs or serving stale data while refreshing.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: LRU vs LFU eviction: which is better for a workload with a few permanently popular items plus a stream of one-off scans?
options: LFU, because frequency protects hot items from being pushed out by scans
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: A large scan can flush an LRU cache of hot items. LFU keeps frequently used ones, though it needs aging to forget items that were once popular.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Which approach is best to make a CDN-cached static asset update immediately on deploy?
options: Version the file name or add a content hash, such as app.3f9c.js
Call the CDN purge API for each user
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: Immutable, hash-named assets can be cached for a year because a new deploy produces new URLs. Only the HTML entry point needs a short TTL.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Push CDN vs pull CDN: which fetches content from the origin only on first request?
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: A pull CDN lazily caches on a miss, so it's simple but the first user pays latency. A push CDN needs you to upload content and suits rarely changing large files.

hld-partitioning:1.prompt: What problem does consistent hashing solve compared with hash(key) % N?
options: Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of the keys rather than almost all
hld-partitioning:1.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing N moves nearly every key and wipes out cache or shard locality. A hash ring moves only the keys between neighbouring nodes.

hld-partitioning:1.prompt: Why add virtual nodes to a consistent hash ring?
options: To spread load more evenly and let stronger machines own more positions
hld-partitioning:1.explanation: A few physical nodes may land unevenly on the ring. Many virtual positions per node smooth the distribution and make rebalancing gradual.

hld-partitioning:0.prompt: Range partitioning on a timestamp key typically creates which problem?
options: A hot partition, as all new writes go to the latest range
hld-partitioning:0.explanation: Hash partitioning spreads writes evenly but loses efficient range queries. Compound keys or bucketing time ranges with a hash prefix can balance them.

hld-partitioning:3.prompt: In leader-follower replication, why can reading from a follower return stale data?
options: Replication is asynchronous, so followers lag behind the leader
Followers are read-only so they are older
Reads always go to the leader
hld-partitioning:3.explanation: This replication lag causes anomalies like not seeing your own write. Read-your-writes can be provided by reading from the leader for recently modified data or tracking a timestamp.

hld-partitioning:3.prompt: What is the main complication of multi-leader replication?
options: Conflicting concurrent writes to the same data in different leaders must be resolved
hld-partitioning:3.explanation: Resolution strategies include last-write-wins, merge functions, CRDTs or application-defined handling. Single-leader avoids conflicts but has one write path.

hld-partitioning:5.prompt: With N = 3 replicas, which R and W settings give strong read-after-write via quorum overlap?
hld-partitioning:5.explanation: R + W > N guarantees that read and write sets overlap in at least one replica holding the latest value. R = 1, W = 1 can read a stale replica.

hld-consistency:0.prompt: What does the CAP theorem say about a network partition?
options: You must choose between consistency and availability for the partitioned system
You can always have all three
hld-consistency:0.explanation: Partitions are not optional in distributed systems, so the real choice is CP (reject or delay requests to stay consistent) or AP (serve possibly stale data). PACELC adds the latency vs consistency trade-off when there is no partition.

hld-consistency:0.prompt: What does PACELC add on top of CAP?
options: Even without a partition, there is a trade-off between latency and consistency
hld-consistency:0.explanation: If Partitioned choose A or C; Else choose Latency or Consistency. It explains why even healthy systems choose weaker consistency for speed.

hld-consistency:2.prompt: In Raft, what does a candidate need to become leader?
options: Votes from a majority of the nodes
A vote from the old leader
hld-consistency:2.explanation: A majority quorum ensures two leaders can't exist in the same term. Clusters therefore use odd sizes like 3 or 5, tolerating 1 or 2 failures respectively.

hld-consistency:4.prompt: Why is the Saga pattern used instead of two-phase commit across microservices?
options: 2PC blocks and requires locks across services, while sagas use local transactions with compensating actions
hld-consistency:4.explanation: A saga chains local transactions and undoes completed steps with compensations on failure. It gives eventual consistency and requires compensations to be idempotent.

hld-consistency:5.prompt: How do you make a payment API safe against client retries?
options: Require an idempotency key and store the result so a repeat returns the same response
hld-consistency:5.explanation: The server records the key with the outcome, so duplicates don't charge twice. Exactly-once effects are built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: A system starts on one server. What is typically the first scaling step in the 'scale from zero to millions' progression?
options: Separate the web tier and the database onto different servers
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: Splitting tiers lets each scale independently, and you then add a load balancer with stateless web servers, database replication, caching, a CDN, and so on.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: Why should web servers be stateless when scaling horizontally?
options: Any server can handle any request, so a load balancer can add or remove instances freely
Stateless servers are faster to write
State is not allowed in HTTP
It removes the need for a database
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: Session data moves to a shared store (Redis, database), which allows autoscaling and rolling deploys without sticky sessions.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: A URL shortener uses 7 characters from [a-zA-Z0-9]. About how many unique URLs can it represent?
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12, which is plenty for years at hundreds of millions of URLs a day. Base-62 encoding of an incrementing id avoids collisions.

hld-url-shortener:0.prompt: Which HTTP redirect should a URL shortener typically use if it wants to track every click?
options: 302 (temporary), so clients request the short URL each time
hld-url-shortener:0.explanation: 301 lets browsers and proxies cache the redirect, so later clicks might never reach your server. 302 keeps analytics accurate at a bit more load.

hld-ratelimiter-idgen:0.prompt: What is the main advantage of the token bucket algorithm for rate limiting?
options: It allows short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a steady average rate
It is exact for every window boundary
hld-ratelimiter-idgen:0.explanation: Tokens refill at a constant rate, and each request spends one. Fixed window counters can allow double the limit at window edges, which sliding window and token bucket avoid.

hld-ratelimiter-idgen:1.prompt: What are the parts of a Twitter Snowflake ID?
options: Timestamp, machine or datacenter id and a per-millisecond sequence
hld-ratelimiter-idgen:1.explanation: Ids are roughly time-sortable and generated without coordination across machines, which suits distributed systems. Clock skew needs handling.

hld-feed-chat:0.prompt: In a news feed system, what is the trade-off of fan-out on write (push)?
options: Fast reads, but heavy write amplification for users with many followers
hld-feed-chat:0.explanation: Pre-computing each follower's feed makes reads cheap, but a celebrity post triggers millions of writes. Many systems use a hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities at read time.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: What does a message queue like Kafka provide beyond a simple in-memory queue?
options: Durable, partitioned, replayable logs with consumer groups for horizontal scaling
hld-messaging:0.explanation: Messages are persisted and ordered within a partition, and consumers track offsets, so they can replay. Ordering across partitions isn't guaranteed.

hld-messaging:0.prompt: Why is a dead-letter queue useful?
options: It parks messages that keep failing so they don't block the main queue and can be inspected
hld-messaging:0.explanation: After a bounded number of retries, poison messages are moved aside for debugging or manual replay.
